texanshootR

running tests until one comes back significant

texanshootR runs a budgeted, seeded specification search over a data frame until some model reaches p <= 0.05, then writes the paper around it.

The name comes from the Texas sharpshooter, who fires at the side of a barn all night and in the morning paints a target around the densest cluster of holes. Each shoot() call opens a wall-clock budget and searches predictor subsets, transformations, interactions, outlier exclusions and subgroup splits. As the budget runs low it moves on to other model families and derived metrics, favouring whatever is almost significant and abandoning specifications that go cold. The seed, R version, package version and a hash of the full search trace are stored on the returned run, so you can replay any saved run exactly and decide which finding to write up.

texanshootR supports:

  • Searching the model space. Eight model families have native fitters, with the heavier ones written in C++ through Rcpp, and a selector escalates from lm to the others as the run comes under pressure (The search engine).
  • Writing it up. A run that clears p <= 0.05 opens a six-stage publication chain: abstract, manuscript, presentation, reviewer response, graphical abstract and funding letter.
  • A research career. Redeemed stages award XP, and the career tier that follows from it decides which model families enter the search. Achievements and a wardrobe of cosmetics come with it.
  • Commentary in the terminal. A YAML message registry, each message tagged with the fallacy it commits, narrates the search.

Installation

The release on CRAN installs as a binary on Windows and macOS, so no build tools are needed:

install.packages("texanshootR")

The development version compiles C++ code, so install the build tools for your operating system first:

Operating system Build tools
Windows Rtools, the version that matches your R version
macOS Run xcode-select --install in Terminal
Debian / Ubuntu Install r-base-dev

Check that R can find the compiler:

pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)

Then install texanshootR:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/texanshootR")

The C++ backend (penalised least squares for gam, a profile-likelihood mixed model for glmm) needs no system libraries; its only compiled dependency is Rcpp, which installs from CRAN with the package.

Usage

  1. Run the search on a data frame with shoot().
  2. Print the run to see the finding, the search behind it and the outputs it unlocked.
  3. Redeem the unlocked stages of the publication chain, starting with abstract().
library(texanshootR)

run <- shoot(mtcars)
#> A finding has cleared threshold. Pipeline armed.
#> Publication chain opened. Next: abstract().
run
#> ================================================================
#> ( -_-) ︻デ═一  ·
#> texanshootR :: run 0001
#> ================================================================
#> 
#> RUN
#> status: publishable result identified
#> career impact: advanced
#> mascot state: composed → resolved
#> 
#> FINDING
#> mpg ~ gear + drat
#> methods: partialling out variation due to am
#> p: 0.045
#> 
#> SEARCH
#> candidate specifications: 3,000
#> model families explored: lm glm rlm
#> modifiers used: +compilation +complexity_shield
#> 
#> OUTPUTS
#> available now: abstract(run)
#> 
#> locked:
#> manuscript()         requires Postdoc
#> presentation()       requires Postdoc
#> reviewer_response()  requires Senior Scientist
#> graphical_abstract() requires Senior Scientist
#> funding()            requires PI
#> 
#> DATA USED
#> exclusion rule: none
#> rows excluded: 0
#> outcome construction: partialling out variation due to am
#> derived metrics: disabled
#> search seed: 1140350788
#> run stored: no

Without a formula, shoot() takes the first numeric column as the outcome and every other column as a predictor. The default budget is 30 seconds of wall-clock time, so a run on another machine may land somewhere else; the stored seed replays it.

abstract(run)

Each generator writes its file to tempdir() and returns the path invisibly. output_dir = or options(texanshootR.output_dir = ...) sends it elsewhere.

The search engine

The seven families of the career ladder each have their own fitter, with no soft dependency on mgcv, lme4 or lavaan:

  • lm: ordinary least squares via .lm.fit()
  • cor: bivariate Pearson, Spearman or Kendall correlation
  • glm: Gaussian, binomial, Poisson or Gamma with a choice of links
  • wls: two-stage feasible weighted least squares
  • gam: penalised B-spline regression with smoothing chosen by GCV, in C++
  • glmm: Gaussian random-intercept mixed model by profile likelihood, in C++
  • sem: single-mediator path model with a Sobel test for the indirect effect

Model-form escalation can also refit a specification with rlm, robust M-estimation with Huber weights. A family selector attaches a fitter to each specification from the run’s escalation state and the shape of the outcome: lm early, glm under pressure, and an occasional forced coercion (binomial on a continuous outcome, Poisson on a rounded one) when the shooter is chasing the next decimal.

The publication chain

A run that clears p <= 0.05 is shippable, and the first shippable run opens the chain. The stages are redeemed in order:

abstract(run)            # one-paragraph deadpan summary
manuscript(run)          # IMRaD draft; Methods match the winning spec
presentation(run)        # 8-slide deck; residual plot on slide 7
reviewer_response(run)   # opens "we thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments"
graphical_abstract(run)  # the figure your PI will retweet
funding(run)             # the next grant, citing the just-shipped finding

Finishing the chain through your unlocked stages adds a length bonus to the XP of each stage. A fresh shoot() mid-chain forfeits the bonus and keeps the partial XP. Locked stages, expired windows, the wrong run and out-of-order calls signal a tx_chain_error whose reason field your tests can branch on. Getting started with texanshootR walks through a chain.

Career and unlocks

Cumulative XP sets how many stages of the chain you can redeem, and your career tier is a label derived from that length. The tier gates which model families enter the search pool:

Chain length New stage XP needed Career tier Families added
1 abstract() 0 Junior Researcher lm
2 manuscript() 5 Postdoc cor, glm
3 presentation() 15 Postdoc none
4 reviewer_response() 30 Senior Scientist wls, gam
5 graphical_abstract() 55 Senior Scientist none
6 funding() 90 PI glmm, sem 
career()        # tier, runs, favourite method, opaque scores
achievements()  # 20 unlockable badges; hidden ones show as ???
wardrobe()      # cosmetic slots (hat, badge, cloak, poncho, lanyard)
progress()      # HUD: chain length, XP, next unlock, live chain window
run_log()       # every run on this profile

The message pack

The terminal commentary comes from a YAML message registry under inst/messages/. Each message carries a trigger phase, a fallacy tag from vocab_tags (such as p_hacking, harking, subgroup_fishing and causal_overreach), a rarity weight, and optional affinities to a mascot state and a model family, so a line about GAMs only fires when the run picked a GAM. validate_messages() checks the registry against the schema in MESSAGE_SCHEMA.md, so adding a message is a YAML edit and a call to it.

Persistent state

Your researcher profile is stored as flat YAML under tools::R_user_dir("texanshootR", "data"), readable and version-controllable. The first interactive save asks before writing anything to disk. With options(texanshootR.save_enabled = FALSE) the package runs without state: every call is independent, and progression stays at Junior Researcher. reset_career(), reset_achievements(), reset_wardrobe() and reset_all() start over (Resetting).
